## Vector Toolkit

Checking a vector file before you trust it, and doing real analysis
with it once you do. Free, no account, nothing ever leaves your
browser. Want the full explanation instead of just the tool? The
[interactive articles](/articles.html) walk through the same
computations in Python and R.

**[Inspect](geospatial-file-inspector.qmd)** →
**[Validate](geojson-shapefile-validator.qmd)** →
**[Check Topology](topology-checker.qmd)** →
**[CRS](crs-inspector.qmd)** →
**[Buffer](buffer-proximity.qmd)**

Five tools are live — Inspect, Validate geometry, Check Topology,
find/convert a CRS, and buffer points/lines/polygons at any distance.

## Raster Toolkit

Reading a GeoTIFF, then computing with it. **[Inspect](raster-inspector.qmd)**
→ **[Calculate](raster-calculator.qmd)** → **[NDVI](ndvi-calculator.qmd)**
→ **[Viewshed](viewshed-calculator.qmd)**: dimensions, bands,
resolution, CRS, NoData, and per-band value ranges first, then combine
two bands into a computed result — a difference map, a Normalized
Difference — shown as a colored overlay and downloadable as a GeoTIFF.
The NDVI tool specializes that same computation for vegetation
health, with red/near-infrared band presets. Viewshed answers a
different question — what's visible from a point, given the terrain
in between — and runs on R (Python is shown only as reference in its
[companion article](/posts/raster-viewshed.html), since no viewshed
implementation is available in this browser's Python runtime).

Got a raster with NoData holes to fill? That's the
**[Raster Gap Filler](raster-gap-filler.qmd)**, listed under
GeoStatistics below, since it fills them by kriging.

## GeoML Toolkit

Machine learning on spatial data — finding groups, and predicting
labels. **[Cluster](spatial-clustering-explorer.qmd)** →
**[Classify](spatial-classifier.qmd)**: find which points form dense
groups with DBSCAN, or train a Random Forest on a labeled column and
predict a full classification surface across the whole area — both
colored on the map, both downloadable. Two tools live in this family;
more are planned.

## Network Toolkit

Turning a line layer into a graph. **[Network from Lines](network-from-lines.qmd)**:
nodes at the line endpoints, edges along the lines, connected
components colored both on the map and in a force-directed diagram —
see exactly how much a snap tolerance changes how many pieces the
network has. One tool live in this family; more are planned.

## GeoStatistics Toolkit

Predicting a continuous surface from sparse point samples, and filling
the gaps in a surface you already have.
**[Kriging Interpolator](kriging-interpolator.qmd)** →
**[Raster Gap Filler](raster-gap-filler.qmd)**: the first predicts a
full surface from scattered measurements by fitting a variogram model
to how similar nearby points really are, not just averaging distance-
weighted neighbors; the second applies the same method to an existing
raster, fitting a variogram on its own valid pixels to fill its
NoData holes, optionally helped by a second, correlated band as a
covariate (cokriging). Both run on R (Python is
shown only as reference in their companion articles —
[kriging](/posts/kriging-soil-sampling.html),
[cokriging](/posts/cokriging-raster-gap-filling.html) — since neither
implementation exists for this browser's Python runtime). Two tools
live in this family; more are planned.
